summary: Describes Bidirectional PIM, a variant of PIM Sparse-Mode that builds bidirectional shared trees for multicast. A Designated Forwarder election on each link lets data flow to the Rendezvous Point and receivers without source-specific state. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A way for group messages to travel along one shared road in both directions, so routers keep less per-sender info.

questions: what is a designated forwarder in pim
how does bidir-pim differ from pim sparse mode
what is the rendezvous point link
subtitle: Multicast shared trees that carry data in both directions, using an elected forwarder on each link instead of per-source state.

tldr.problem: In PIM Sparse-Mode, data from a source reaches the shared tree either by encapsulating it in Register messages to the Rendezvous Point, which costs processing, bandwidth and delay, or by building source-specific state along the path, which costs protocol and memory.
tldr.mechanism: BIDIR-PIM elects one Designated Forwarder (DF) per Rendezvous Point Address on every link. The DF picks up upstream traffic and passes it toward the root and carries downstream traffic onto its link, so packets flow natively along shared tree state in both directions.
tldr.outcome: No encapsulation, no source state and no data-driven protocol events are needed. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436.

today: RFC 5015 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted. It has been updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436, so read those alongside it.

sections.title: Why Bidirectional Trees
sections.content:
BIDIR-PIM is a variant of PIM Sparse-Mode (PIM-SM, RFC 4601) that builds bidirectional shared trees connecting multicast sources and receivers. In PIM-SM each group has a shared tree rooted at a Rendezvous Point (RP), and data gets from a source to the RP in one of two ways.

First, the source's first-hop router encapsulates packets in Register messages unicast to the RP, which decapsulates them and sends them down the tree. Second, a later switch to forwarding builds source-specific state on every router between the source and the RP. The RFC says encapsulation brings significant processing, bandwidth and delay overheads, and source-specific forwarding has extra protocol and memory requirements.

BIDIR-PIM drops both. Packets are forwarded natively from a source toward the RP using shared tree state, with no data-driven events. The spec assumes you already know PIM-SM and defines shared parts, such as Hello and Join/Prune formats, only by reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way either wrapped every message in a parcel to send it to the center, or made every road keep a note about every sender. The new way lets messages just drive along the shared road.

sections.title: Key Terms: RPA, RPL and the Designated Forwarder
sections.content:
The Rendezvous Point Address (RPA) is the root of the tree for a range of groups. It must be routable from every router in the domain, but it does not have to belong to a real router interface, unlike PIM-SM. The Rendezvous Point Link (RPL) is the physical link the RPA belongs to. All traffic for the groups of an RPA is forwarded on its RPL, and the RPL is the one link where no DF election happens.

Upstream means toward the root (the RPA) and downstream means away from it. The Designated Forwarder (DF) is the single router on each link, per RPA, with the best route to the RPA as judged by metrics from the Multicast Routing Information Base (MRIB). The DF forwards downstream traffic onto its link, forwards upstream traffic from the link toward the RPL, and handles Joins from downstream routers and local receivers learned through IGMP or MLD.

A router learns which groups use an RPA by static configuration or by an automatic mechanism such as the PIM Bootstrap mechanism (BSR) or Auto-RP. The RFC also explains that the RPA can be set to a router's loopback interface to behave like PIM-SM with a single RP.
sections.plainLanguage: The root of the tree is like the town square everyone's messages meet at. On each street, one neighbor is chosen as the helper, the one with the shortest way to the square.

sections.title: Forwarding Data in Both Directions
sections.content:
The DF is the only router that forwards downstream traffic onto its link, and the only router that picks up upstream traffic from it. A packet to group G arriving on interface iif is accepted if iif is the RPF interface toward the RPA (a downstream packet) or the router is the DF on iif (an upstream packet). The router then forwards it on the outgoing interface list for G minus the incoming interface.

The outgoing list combines three things: the RPF interface toward the RPA, interfaces with (*,G) Join state where the router is DF, and interfaces with local members where the router is DF.

This design removes special cases. Data from a directly connected source is simply picked up by the DF and forwarded upstream, so no directly-connected-source check is needed. Source-only branches, which lead to no receivers, need no group state at all, only RPA state. An implementation may keep group state there for accounting or performance, but doing so brings back data-driven events.
sections.plainLanguage: A message is only passed along if it comes from the road leading to the town square, or from a street where this router is the chosen helper. That way two routers never both pass the same message and cause loops.

sections.title: Join and Prune Messages
sections.content:
Receivers' last-hop routers that are DF on a link with receivers send (*,G) Joins hop by hop toward the RPA until they reach a router on the RPL. Joins are sent on the RPF interface toward the RPA and addressed to the DF there.

On the receiving side, each interface and group has a small state machine with three states: NoInfo, Join and PrunePending. A Join starts or restarts the Expiry Timer, set from the HoldTime in the message. A Prune starts the PrunePendingTimer, which is the J/P Override Interval when the interface has more than one neighbor and zero otherwise. When it expires, the router stops forwarding and may send a PruneEcho, a Prune sent to itself so that a lost override has another chance. A message whose RP address does not match the router's RPA for the group is silently dropped.

Upstream, the router is either Not Joined or Joined. It sends a Join when it wants the tree and a Prune when it no longer does, refreshes with a timer (default 60 seconds), suppresses its own Join if it hears another to the same upstream neighbor, and overrides a Prune it sees. A change of RPF interface or of DF triggers a Prune toward the old neighbor and a Join toward the new one.
sections.plainLanguage: When someone wants to listen, their helper keeps telling the next helper up the road, 'still here, keep sending.' If the reminders stop, or someone says 'no thanks' and nobody objects, the flow stops.

sections.title: Electing the Designated Forwarder
sections.content:
The election is per RPA, not per group, so a few elections cover many groups. The winner should be the router with the best unicast metric to the RPA, compared with the same rules as the PIM-SM assert process. A router whose own route to the RPA goes out of the link being elected always advertises an infinite metric there, because it cannot offer a way toward the RPL.

Four messages are used. Offer advertises a router's metric when it thinks it can win. Winner announces the DF and its metric. Backoff is sent by the DF to acknowledge a better offer and tell routers with worse offers to wait. Pass hands over responsibility to the router that made the best offer, naming both the old and new DF.

At startup, routers send Offers. A router that has advertised its metric Election_Robustness times without hearing a better offer sends a Winner and becomes DF. When a non-DF's metric becomes better than the DF's, it sends Offers; the DF replies with Backoff and, before the Backoff_Period ends, a Pass. The old DF stops at the moment it sends the Pass, and the new DF takes over when it receives it.

The design deliberately leans toward discarding DF information and suspending forwarding when things are unclear, because two DFs on one link could create loops. Optional safeguards include marking a missing Pass and having the DF periodically repeat its Winner message.
sections.plainLanguage: The neighbors on a street each shout how short their way to the square is. The shortest one becomes the helper. If someone else later finds a shorter way, the helper politely hands over the job, so there is never a moment with two helpers.

sections.title: Packet Formats and Timers
sections.content:
All PIM control messages use IP protocol number 103. BIDIR-PIM election messages are multicast with TTL 1 to the ALL-PIM-ROUTERS group, which is 224.0.0.13 in IPv4 and ff02::d in IPv6. They share a common header with PIM version 2, Type 10, and a Subtype of 1 (Offer), 2 (Winner), 3 (Backoff) or 4 (Pass), followed by a checksum, the RP address, the sender's metric preference and the sender's metric. Backoff adds the offering router's address, metric preference and metric plus an interval in milliseconds, and Pass adds the new winner's address, metric preference and metric.

Routers also advertise a new Hello option, Bidirectional Capable (OptionType 22, length 0), which MUST appear in every Hello from a BIDIR-PIM router. If a neighbor's Hello lacks it, the error must be logged in a rate-limited way.

Default timers: Offer_Period 100 ms between repeated Offer and Winner messages, Backoff_Period 1 second, Election_Robustness 3, J/P Override Interval 3 seconds and t_periodic 60 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The helpers talk with short, standard notes, and a special badge in their hello says 'I know how to do this job.'

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
BIDIR-PIM messages are link-local, so attacks need a directly connected node or the cooperation of a directly connected router. Hello and Join/Prune messages are the same as in PIM-SM, and their security considerations are in RFC 4601. The DF election messages are new, and forging them lets an attacker win the election by claiming the best metric, impersonate another router with an Offer, Winner or Pass, or keep the election from converging with an endless stream of Offers.

Authenticating the source of election messages defeats impersonation, and spoofed messages MUST then be discarded with a rate-limited warning. Routers SHOULD also check the destination MAC address of election messages, to stop an attacker from using unicast MAC addresses to give different routers different views of the DF, although that fails on links without layer-2 multicast. A router SHOULD offer a way to limit the neighbors it accepts Join/Prune, Assert and election messages from, and SHOULD NOT accept messages from a router it has not yet received a valid Hello from.

The recommended mechanism is IPsec in transport mode using the Authentication Header, as in PIM-SM. The RFC notes that access control for sources is generally only feasible for receivers in BIDIR-PIM, since sources can send without routers detecting them.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the helpers just trust each other's notes, a faker could pretend to be the best helper. Signing the notes and only listening to known neighbors stops that.
